title: Pizza, Pasta, Soup: Who Likes All Three? | AMC 8-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: 24 kid tokens (simple circles with faces) in a 6×4 grid, numbered 1–24 small. Food icons pizza 🍕, pasta 🍝, soup 🥣 drawn as simple colored badges (not emoji fonts if they don't render; colored rounded squares with labels 'pizza', 'pasta', 'soup'). Line 2: three overlapping Venn circles appear then get crossed out with a friendly 'no need!'. Line 3: Vantee title card.
lines: Twenty-four kids, three foods. What's the fewest kids who could like all three?
You might reach for a big Venn diagram. There's a much quicker trick.
Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's count the kids who say no.

scenes.visual: Question text left; kid grid right with food badges and counts: 'pizza 20', 'pasta 18', 'soup 16' appearing on lines 3-5. Line 6: chips 0, 4, 6, 14, 16.
lines: Here's the question.
In a class of twenty-four kids,
Twenty kids like pizza,
Eighteen kids like pasta,
and sixteen like soup. What is the smallest possible number of kids who like all three?
Here are the five choices. Take a good look.

scenes.visual: Line 1: the three counts as cards. Line 2: words 'smallest POSSIBLE' marked. Line 3: two different arrangements flicker (some kids switching likes) to suggest 'we choose the arrangement'.
lines: So what do we know? Twenty-four kids, and three counts: twenty, eighteen and sixteen.
We want the smallest POSSIBLE number who like all three.
So we get to arrange who likes what, and try to make that group as small as we can.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; counts visible.
lines: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.visual: Kid grid. Line 2: row '24 − 20 = 4' ; 4 kids get a red 'no pizza' tag. Line 3: '24 − 18 = 6', '24 − 16 = 8' rows. Line 4: plain text 'say no to something → not all three'.
lines: Welcome back! Here's the strategy: count the kids who say no.
Twenty like pizza, so four kids don't.
Eighteen like pasta, so six don't. Sixteen like soup, so eight don't.
Any kid who says no to even one food is NOT in the all-three group.

scenes.visual: Line 1: kids 1–4 tagged 'no pizza' (red), 5–10 'no pasta' (orange), 11–18 'no soup' (blue): each kid gets exactly one tag, no kid has two. Line 2: '4 + 6 + 8 = 18'. Line 3: '24 − 18 = 6'; kids 19–24 glow green 'all three'. Line 4: check row 'pizza: 24 − 4 = 20 ✓, pasta: 24 − 6 = 18 ✓, soup: 24 − 8 = 16 ✓'. Line 5: answer badge '6' with chime at line end, choice C highlighted.
lines: To make the all-three group small, give the no's to different kids. No kid says no twice.
Then four plus six plus eight is eighteen kids who say no to something.
That leaves twenty-four minus eighteen, six kids who say no to nothing. They like all three!
Check the counts: twenty like pizza, eighteen like pasta, sixteen like soup. It works.
And we can't do better, because there are only eighteen no's to hand out.
The answer is six. That's Choice C!

scenes.visual: Two horizontal bars of length 24 slots. Line 2: pizza bar 20 slots from the left, pasta bar 18 slots from the right; overlap highlighted: '20 + 18 = 38', '38 − 24 = 14'. Line 3: new bar 'pizza and pasta: 14' vs soup bar 16 from the other end: '14 + 16 = 30', '30 − 24 = 6'. Line 4: small card 'overlap ≥ a + b − total'.
lines: Here's another way: combine two foods at a time.
Pizza and pasta: twenty plus eighteen is thirty-eight.
That's fourteen more than twenty-four, so at least fourteen kids like both.
Now add soup. Fourteen plus sixteen is thirty.
That's six more than twenty-four, so at least six like all three. Same answer!
When would you pick this way? When you want to see the overlap shrink one food at a time.

scenes.visual: Choice chips; wrong ones turn red. Line 2: '24 − 20 = 4'. Line 3: '16 = soup group'. Line 4: the 14 from solution 2 with 'stopped too early'. Line 5: chip 0 with '18 no's for 24 kids: 6 left over'.
lines: Now let's look at the wrong answers. Each one is a trap.
Choice B, four, is the number of kids who don't like pizza. That's only one of the counts.
Choice E, sixteen, is the soup group.
That's the biggest the all-three group could be, not the smallest.
Choice D, fourteen, is the pizza and pasta overlap. That's what you get if you stop before adding soup.
Choice A, zero, would need twenty-four no's. There are only eighteen, so six kids must like everything.
So here's a great habit. To find the smallest group that says yes to everything, count the no's.

scenes.visual: New card: '30 kids: cats 25, dogs 22, fish 20, birds 27'.
lines: Ready for a challenge? Now there are four things to like.
In a class of thirty kids, twenty-five like cats and twenty-two like dogs.
Twenty like fish, and twenty-seven like birds.
What is the smallest possible number of kids who like all four?

scenes.visual: Pause card, countdown, variant card visible.
lines: Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: Rows per line: '30 − 25 = 5', '30 − 22 = 8', '30 − 20 = 10', '30 − 27 = 3'; then '5 + 8 + 10 + 3 = 26'; then '30 − 26 = 4' answer badge with chime at line end.
lines: Let's count the no's. Five don't like cats, eight don't like dogs.
Ten don't like fish, and three don't like birds.
Give them to different kids: five plus eight plus ten plus three is twenty-six no's in all.
Thirty minus twenty-six is four. At least four kids like all four!
Here's the cool part. A fourth favorite didn't make it harder, just one more count.
If you got four, amazing work!

scenes.visual: Summary card: 'fewest who like ALL = total − (sum of the no's)' with the kid grid icon.
lines: Here's the big idea to remember.
Count how many kids say no to each thing, and give the no's to different kids.
Everyone left over must like everything. That's the smallest the group can be.
I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
